source.version: Journal version of record, Frontiers in Psychology 17:1847432, published 17 June 2026; DOI 10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1847432 (p. 1).
source.title_on_document: Effects of integrating a structured design thinking strategy into generative AI-supported design learning on students? design achievement, creative self-efficacy, and problem-solving skills

supplement.holds: Supplementary Table S1 describes the Double Diamond-Based Design Operation Sheet (DDDOS): stage objectives, self-monitoring questions, suggested GAI use, and stage completion checks (p. 5, section 3.3). The supplement is not included in this PDF and was not inspected. The main text does not identify supplementary outcome statistics or standard errors.

paper_design_summary: In a university animation course in China, students were randomly assigned to generative AI with a structured Double Diamond design-thinking strategy, the same AI tools without the strategy, or traditional design learning; they independently produced card-game character designs (p. 4, sections 3.1?3.3). The study analyzed 120 students, with 40 per group, and two design instructors rated the final artworks using a rubric combining creativity and other design-quality criteria (p. 8, section 3.4; p. 9, Table 1). Creative self-efficacy and perceived problem-solving were measured using questionnaires rather than scored creative outputs (p. 8, section 3.4).

assignment.what_was_assigned: Students were randomly assigned to GAI-SDTS, GAI, or TDL after three existing classes were selected by cluster sampling from six classes. They were then reorganized into new mixed-class groups by condition and worked independently. Individual random assignment is explicit despite the authors calling the design quasi-experimental (pp. 3?4, sections 3.1?3.2).
assignment.quote: All students in the selected classes were then randomly assigned to one of three groups:
assignment.locator: p. 4, section 3.2, Population and sampling; also p. 4, section 3.1.

arms.name: GAI-SDTS
arms.description: Deepseek and Dreamina with a Double Diamond-Based Design Operation Sheet guiding Discover, Define, Develop, and Deliver; the sheet supplies stage objectives and self-monitoring checks (pp. 5?7, section 3.3). Initial group N is shown in p. 9, Figure 8; analyzed N is in p. 9, Table 1.

arms.name: GAI
arms.description: Free use of the same Deepseek and Dreamina tools without structured design-thinking guidance (p. 5, section 3.3). Initial group N is shown in p. 9, Figure 8; analyzed N is in p. 9, Table 1.

arms.name: TDL
arms.description: Traditional design learning: printed materials and online references, hand-drawn sketches, and traditional digital software such as Photoshop; no GAI or explicit design-thinking strategy (p. 5, section 3.3; p. 9, section 3.5). Initial group N is shown in p. 9, Figure 8; analyzed N is in p. 9, Table 1.

participants.exclusions: No exclusions or attrition are stated. Section 3.2 reports 120 participants and says all students were randomly assigned; Figure 8 shows 40 in each initial group, and Table 1 analyzes 40 per group. No separate participant-flow accounting is provided (p. 4, section 3.2; p. 9, Figure 8 and Table 1).
participants.who: Second-year undergraduate animation majors at a university in central China (p. 4, section 3.2).
participants.quote: A total of 120 students aged between 19 and 22 years (M = 20.4, SD = 0.84) participated in the experiment.
participants.locator: p. 4, section 3.2, for population, total and random assignment; p. 9, Figure 8, for initial group counts; p. 9, Table 1, for analyzed counts.

ai_tool.name_model: Deepseek and Dreamina; specific model versions not stated.
ai_tool.how_used: Deepseek supported dialogue, character ideation, concept and prompt refinement, and final design statements; Dreamina supported text-to-image and image-to-image generation, alternative character visuals, refinement, and export. Both AI groups used these tools while producing the final scored artworks, with stage-specific guidance only in GAI-SDTS (pp. 5?7, section 3.3; p. 9, section 3.5). The single role code emphasizes image generation; text-based open chat and refinement were also used.

task.description: Independently design and create a distinctive card-game character with clear personality traits, progressing through character exploration, definition, creation, and presentation (p. 4, sections 3.2?3.3; p. 5, Figure 2).
task.duration: Four-week intensive practical course, October 20 to November 14, 2025 (p. 4, section 3.2). The experimental schedule places familiarization and pretests in Week 1, design production in Weeks 2?5, and grading of final artworks and questionnaires in Week 6 (pp. 8?9, section 3.5; p. 9, Figure 8).

outcomes.name: Design achievement: composite rating of final character artwork
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: The rubric assesses Technical Skill, Adherence to Theme, Composition and Design, Creativity, and Detail Quality and Workload, each rated from 1 (lowest) to 5 (highest). Two instructors with 8 years of design teaching experience independently rated anonymized, randomly ordered final submissions; Kendall?s W = 0.94, p < 0.001 (p. 8, section 3.4). Only the overall design-achievement score is reported (p. 9, Table 1), with no separate Creativity subscore or explicit rule for combining dimensions and raters. Coded usefulness because the codebook includes output quality: this is a broad design-quality composite containing creativity, not a standalone overall-creativity rating. The ANOVA compares student scores, with one final design per student (p. 4, sections 3.2?3.3; p. 9, sections 3.5 and 4.1).

contrasts.reported: GAI M = 18.65, SD = 7.41, N = 40; TDL M = 16.13, SD = 6.85, N = 40. The text reports Tukey?s HSD: GAI > TDL, p < 0.001. The omnibus ANOVA across all three groups is F = 43.28, p < 0.001; this is not a pairwise F statistic. No standardized effect, contrast standard error, or confidence interval is printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 9, Table 1 and section 4.1, Design achievement results.

company_involvement.description: No company involvement is reported. Both authors list a university affiliation; the authors state that no financial support was received and that there were no commercial or financial relationships constituting a potential conflict of interest.

eligibility.reason: Students were explicitly randomly assigned to AI-assisted design conditions or traditional no-AI design learning and regrouped across their original classes (p. 4, sections 3.1?3.2). The experiment analyzed 120 people, with 40 per group (p. 4, section 3.2; p. 9, Table 1). Final creative design outputs were rated by design instructors using a rubric that explicitly includes Creativity (p. 8, section 3.4). The reported outcome is the broader design-quality composite, coded usefulness; no isolated creativity effect can be extracted. Despite the quasi-experimental label on pp. 3?4, the described individual random assignment in a university course supports field_rct. AI was available during production of the graded final artworks (pp. 5?7, section 3.3; p. 9, section 3.5; p. 11, section 5.1).

one_line_finding: Among 120 analyzed students, mean final design-achievement scores were 20.90 (SD 7.64) with structured AI use, 18.65 (SD 7.41) with free AI use, and 16.13 (SD 6.85) with traditional learning, with all pairwise comparisons reported as p < 0.001 (p. 9, Table 1 and section 4.1).
open_questions: The authors label the study quasi-experimental but explicitly describe individual random assignment and mixed-class regrouping; the randomization sequence and implementation are not described (pp. 3?4, sections 3.1?3.2).

Separate Creativity-dimension results and the rule for combining the dimensions and the two raters are not given; these would clarify what fraction of the composite difference reflects creativity (p. 8, section 3.4; p. 9, Table 1).

Verify the printed design-achievement means, SDs, omnibus F = 43.28, and all-pairs p < 0.001 claims against the underlying data; they appear internally inconsistent. All reported values are preserved exactly, and no replacement statistics or effect sizes have been computed (p. 9, Table 1 and section 4.1).
notes: Full markdown conversion read through the references, and PDF figures and tables inspected. Complete reported-outcome inventory: design achievement (p. 9, Table 1); creative self-efficacy total, creative ideas self-efficacy, and creative performance self-efficacy (p. 10, Table 2); problem-solving skills total, problem-solving confidence, approach-avoidance style, and personal control (p. 11, Table 3). Only design achievement enters the outcomes array: the other measures are self-report questionnaires (p. 8, section 3.4). The individual artwork-rubric dimensions have no separately reported results. No across-people diversity or unassisted after-AI output outcome is reported. Week 6 grading uses the final artworks produced during the intervention, rather than a new unassisted task (pp. 8?9, section 3.5); the discussion explicitly notes AI-generated and AI-refined artifacts (p. 11, section 5.1). Initial arm counts come from the groups shown before pretests in Figure 8; analyzed arm counts come from Table 1 (p. 9). The TDL contrast is coded ai_vs_bau because traditional software and reference materials comprise the usual design-learning condition. Figure 1 labels design achievement ANCOVA and the questionnaire outcomes ANOVA, whereas the Results and Tables 1?3 describe the reverse; extraction follows the Results and actual table titles (p. 4, Figure 1; pp. 9?11). No reuse of another paper?s participants is stated; the Bian et al. rubric citation identifies an adapted instrument, not a reused sample (p. 8, section 3.4). Raw data are said to be available from the authors, but no public data or code URL is supplied (p. 14, Data availability statement).
